A “yes” vote on 28 of these measures would limit data center development through policies such as bans or moratoriums. A “yes” vote on the remaining 13 measures would facilitate data center development through policies like zoning.
Voters have already decided six measures this year and, in each case, a majority of voters favored greater limits on data center development, either by approving new restrictions or requirements or by rejecting a measure that would have facilitated or supported development. Including these measures, and three that voters will decide after Nov. 3, Ballotpedia is covering 50 local ballot measures (https://ballotpedia.org/Data_center-related_ballot_measures,_2026) in 13 states related to data centers this year.
Ohio voters will decide on 21 measures, more than any other state. Illinois follows with seven measures. Maine voters will decide four, and Kansas voters will decide three. Voters in California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, and Wisconsin will decide one each.
State policies on data centers
State and local governments can affect data center construction through policy actions like permitting, zoning, and tax incentives. As of April 2026, 38 states (https://www.ncsl.org/state-legislatures-news/details/does-your-state-offer-data-center-tax-incentives) had created tax incentives to encourage data center construction.
State and local governments can also use some of these policy actions to prevent or limit data center construction, for example through moratoriums (temporary halts) on issuing permits for new projects. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (https://ballotpedia.org/Kathy_Hochul) (D) issued (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/14/nyregion/new-york-data-center-moratorium-hochul.html) an executive order (https://www.governor.ny.gov/sites/default/files/2026-07/EO_62.pdf) for the first state-level moratorium on data center construction. This one-year moratorium barred state regulators from issuing permits for new data centers expected to use 50 megawatts or more of electricity. Other states have also issued moratoriums on administrative measures like tax breaks (https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/gov-jb-pritzker-to-suspend-tax-breaks-for-data-centers-urging-more-discussion/) and environmental permits (https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/21/texas-data-center-moratorium-water-energy/) for data center construction.
What the Nov. 3 ballot measures would do
Twenty-eight measures, if approved, would limit data center development:
Seventeen would ban data centers. Twelve of these would ban data centers above a certain size threshold. For example, one measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Ottawa,_Kansas,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Kansas would ban data centers using more than 25 megawatts of electricity. Five would ban all data centers.
Three would issue six-month moratoriums on data center development. One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Wells,_Maine,_Article_5,_Data_Center_Moratorium_Measure_(November_2026)) for a moratorium in Wells, Maine, would also (https://wellstown.org/DocumentCenter/View/8514/November-3-2026-Special-Town-Meeting-Warrant?bidId=&p=9) retroactively "nullify any final permit, license, or other approval of a new or expanded Data Center issued by a municipal reviewing authority within 45 days of the effective date."
Two measures in Ohio would establish zoning regulations for unincorporated areas of the local jurisdictions. If the measures are successful and the areas are covered by zoning regulations, they would have to be zoned for a use consistent with data center construction (such as industrial) for a project to be built there.
One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Grove_City,_Ohio,_Issue_28,_Voter_Approval_Requirements_for_Certain_Developments_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Ohio would require voter approval for data center projects above land, water, and power use thresholds, while another (https://ballotpedia.org/Janesville,_Wisconsin,_Require_Voter_Approval_for_Development_of_GM/JATCO_Site_Exceeding_$450_Million_Initiative_(November_2026)) measure in Wisconsin would require voter approval for a specific data center project if it costs more than $450 million.
A measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Harwood,_North_Dakota,_Industrial_Development_Review_Requirements_Initiative_(November_2026)) in North Dakota would require independent professional review and a public hearing for projects exceeding various land area, power, and water use thresholds, as well as projects requiring a major air quality permit.
A measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Perry,_Ohio,_Issue_16,_Hyperscale_Data_Center_Tax_Incentive_Financial_Guarantee_Requirement_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Ohio would require data center developers receiving tax incentives to provide financial guarantees to the community.
Two non-binding measures in Illinois would express voter disapproval of data center projects.
Thirteen measures, if approved, would facilitate data center development:
One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Boulder_City,_Nevada,_Question_1,_Allow_Data_Centers_in_Eldorado_Valley_Transfer_Area_Measure_(November_2026)) in Nevada would add data centers as an approved use for a particular area of land.
One (https://ballotpedia.org/Ashville,_Ohio,_Data_Center_EdgeConneX_Development_Term_Summary_Referendum_(November_2026)) measure in Ohio would uphold a town agreement with a specific data center company.
Four measures in Wilmington, Ohio would rezone specific areas of land from residential to industrial uses, allowing data center construction at these sites. According to WCPO News (https://www.wcpo.com/news/local-news/wilmington-residents-take-aim-at-industrial-zoning-for-data-centers-with-ballot-referendum), a specific data center company may build on this land if it is rezoned.
Seven non-binding measures in Illinois, New Jersey, and Ohio would express voter approval of data center projects.
Voters in four states have already voted on six data center-related measures.
On March 10, voters in Canterbury, New Hampshire, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Canterbury,_New_Hampshire,_Article_4,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Measure_(March_2026)) a ban on data centers 83.6% to 16.4%.
On April 7, voters in Port Washington, Wisconsin, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Port_Washington,_Wisconsin,_Require_Voter_Approval_for_Tax_Incremental_Districts_Exceeding_$10_Million_Initiative_(April_2026)) an initiative 66.4% to 33.6% requiring voter approval for the city to create a Tax Incremental District if projects in the district cost $10 million or more.
On June 2, voters in Monterey Park, California, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Monterey_Park,_California,_Measure_NDC,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Measure_(June_2026)) a ban 88.3% to 11.7%.

State Democratic and Republican parties took opposing positions on 70 ballot measures and agreed on six in 2026
Of the 164 statewide ballot measures that voters have or will decide this year, there were six that state Democratic and Republican parties agreed on and 70 that they disagreed on. Fifty-two measures received support or opposition from only one party. Thirty-six measures did not receive support or opposition from either party.
Republicans supported 50 that Democrats opposed, and Democrats supported 20 that Republicans opposed. Both parties agreed in their support of three measures and opposition to three others.
Overall, Republican parties supported 80 measures (48.8%), opposed 30 (18.3%), and were neutral or had no position on 54 (32.9%). Democratic parties supported 36 measures (22.0%), opposed 58 (35.4%), and were neutral or had no position on 70 (42.7%).
Voters will decide 145 measures on Nov. 3. The other 19 appeared on ballots earlier this year.
Of the 70 measures state parties disagreed on, legislators put 41 (58.6%) on the ballot, and 29 (41.4%) were citizen initiatives, including veto referendums. Some common issues the parties disagreed on were:
Voter ID (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_voter_ID,_2026) : Republicans supported and Democrats opposed measures in Arizona (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_144,_Voter_Identification_and_Citizenship_Voting_Requirements_Amendment_(2026)), California (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_39,_Voter_Identification,_Citizenship_Verification,_and_Registered_Voter_List_Administration_Initiative_(2026)), Colorado (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Amendment_84,_Require_Voter_Identification_Number_for_Mail-In_Ballots_Initiative_(2026)), North Carolina (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment_(2026)), and Ohio (https://ballotpedia.org/Ohio_Issue_3,_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment_(2026)) that would establish or expand voter identification requirements in state constitutions. The Nevada Republicans supported Question 7 (https://ballotpedia.org/Nevada_Question_7,_Require_Voter_Identification_Initiative_(2026)), with no position recorded for Democrats. The Oklahoma Democratic Party opposed State Question 846 (https://ballotpedia.org/Oklahoma_State_Question_846,_Voter_Identification_Requirement_Amendment_(August_2026)), with no position recorded for Republicans.
Abortion policy (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_abortion_policy,_2026) : Democrats supported and Republicans opposed measures in Idaho (https://ballotpedia.org/Idaho_Proposition_1,_Reproductive_Freedom_and_Privacy_Act_Initiative_(2026)) and Virginia (https://ballotpedia.org/Virginia_Question_1,_Right_to_Reproductive_Freedom_Amendment_(2026)), which would establish statutory and constitutional rights related to abortion, respectively. Republicans supported, and Democrats opposed, Missouri Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)), which would repeal the constitutional right to reproductive freedom voters approved in 2024 and prohibit abortion with specified exceptions, among other changes. The Nevada Democratic Party supported Question 6 (https://ballotpedia.org/Nevada_Question_6,_Right_to_Abortion_Initiative_(2026)), which would establish a constitutional right to abortion, with no position recorded for the Republican Party.
Sex-based school sports requirements (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_sex-based_sports_eligibility_and_medical_procedures_for_transgender_minors,_2026): Republicans supported and Democrats opposed all four measures that would establish sex-based requirements for school sports in Arizona (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_318,_Require_All_Schools_and_Athletic_Associations_to_Restrict_Sports_Participation_and_Access_to_Private_Spaces_Based_on_Sex_Measure_(2026)), Colorado (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_134,_Sex_Requirement_for_School_and_College_Sports_Initiative_(2026)), Nebraska (https://ballotpedia.org/Nebraska_Initiative_Measure_442,_Sex_Requirement_for_School_and_College_Sports_Initiative_(2026)), and Washington (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Initiative_638,_Sex_Verification_Requirements_for_Female_School_Sports_Initiative_(2026)).
Medical procedures for transgender minors (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_sex-based_sports_eligibility_and_medical_procedures_for_transgender_minors,_2026): Republicans supported and Democrats opposed Colorado Proposition 135 (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_135,_Prohibit_Surgeries_for_Treatment_in_Response_to_Minors%27_Perception_of_Sex_or_Gender_Measure_(2026)) and Missouri Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)), both of which would prohibit certain medical procedures for transgender minors.
Income and wealth taxes (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_income_and_wealth_taxes,_2026) : Democrats supported and Republicans opposed California Proposition 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)), which would extend higher-income tax rates for education funding; California Proposition 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)), which would impose a one-time wealth tax; and Colorado Amendment 87 (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Amendment_87,_Establish_Graduated_Income_Tax_and_Dedicate_New_Revenue_to_Education,_Healthcare,_and_Childcare_Initiative_(2026)), which would replace the flat income tax with graduated rates. Republicans supported and Democrats opposed measures to restrict, reduce, or repeal income or wealth taxes in California (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_(2026)), Colorado (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_136,_Establish_4.4%25_Cap_on_Individual_and_Corporate_Income_Tax_Rates_Initiative_(2026)), Iowa (https://ballotpedia.org/Iowa_Amendment_1,_Two-Thirds_Legislative_Vote_Requirement_for_Income_Tax_Increase_Bills_Amendment_(2026)), Missouri (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_5,_Income_Tax_Elimination_and_Sales_Tax_Changes_Amendment_(August_2026)), North Carolina (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Reduce_Income_Tax_Rate_Cap_from_7%25_to_3.5%25_Amendment_(2026)), and Washington (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Initiative_645,_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)).
Democratic and Republican parties in the same state supported:
California Proposition 38 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_38,_Immunology_and_Immunotherapy_Research_Funding_Initiative_(2026)), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Louisiana Amendment 7 (https://ballotpedia.org/Louisiana_Amendment_7,_Use_Public_Funds_for_Drinking_Water_Utility_Service_Lines_Amendment_(2026)) , which would amend the state constitution to authorize public funds for maintaining drinking water utility service lines affected by hazardous materials on property owned by utility customers.
Massachusetts Question 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_1,_Public_Records_Requirements_for_Legislature_and_Governor%E2%80%99s_Office_Initiative_(2026)), which would make records that the Legislature and governor’s office hold subject to the state’s public records law with certain exceptions.
Democratic and Republican parties in the same state opposed:
California Proposition 44 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_44,_Spending_Requirements_for_Federally_Qualified_Health_Centers_Initiative_(2026)), which would require nonprofit federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of their annual total revenue on expenses that advance the health center’s mission.
Colorado Proposition 137 (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_137,_Retain_Sporting_Goods_Sales_Tax_Revenue_for_Conservation_and_Wildfire_Prevention_Fund_Initiative_(2026)), which would allow the state to retain and spend sales tax revenue from sporting goods and equipment on water, land, forests, wildfire prevention, and outdoor recreation rather than refunding it under the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights (TABOR).
Massachusetts Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_3,_Top-Two_Primary_Elections_Initiative_(2026)), which would replace separate political party primaries for state elections with a single top-two primaries listing all candidates on the same ballot, regardless of political affiliation.
Legislative votes and party positions differed on five measures
State Democratic parties opposed two measures that Democratic state legislators largely supported in placing on the ballot. 96.3% of Democratic legislators supported California Proposition 43 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_43,_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Local_Special_Tax_Initiatives_and_Property_Tax_Initiative_Prohibition_Amendment_(2026)). It would require two-thirds voter approval for citizen-initiated local special taxes and prohibit local jurisdictions and ballot initiatives from enacting certain property taxes. 100% of Democratic legislators supported Utah Constitutional Amendment A (https://ballotpedia.org/Utah_Constitutional_Amendment_A,_Publication_Requirements_for_Constitutional_Amendments_Measure_(2026)). It would require proposed constitutional amendments to be published for 60 days before the election in a manner that the legislature specifies. It would replace the requirement for newspaper publication in each county.
State Republican parties opposed three measures that Republican state legislators largely supported in placing on the ballot. 100% of Republican legislators supported New Mexico’s Bond Question 2 (https://ballotpedia.org/New_Mexico_Bond_Question_2,_Library_Acquisition_Bond_Issue_(2026)) and Bond Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/New_Mexico_Bond_Question_3,_Higher_Education_Improvements_Bond_Issue_(2026)). Question 2 would authorize up to $20 million in bonds for academic, public school, tribal, and public library acquisitions. Question 3 would authorize up to $230 million in bonds for capital improvements and acquisitions at higher education institutions, special schools, and tribal schools. A statewide property tax would fund both bonds. 95.1% of Republican legislators supported Constitutional Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/New_Mexico_Board_of_Regents_Nominating_Committees_Amendment_(2026)). It would establish regents nominating committees, require student appointees to come from lists that student governing bodies provide, and prohibit non-student appointees from changing political parties during the 12 months preceding appointment.
No measures received state-party support when a majority of that party’s legislators voted against putting them on the ballot.

Next, we have a few questions to ask you about the state propositions on the November ballot.
19. [likely voters only] Proposition 1 is called “Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.” It authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance. Fiscal impact: increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child and Family Services. Opponents: None submitted.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
60% yes
38% no
2% don’t know
20. [likely voters only] Proposition 2 is called “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.” It increases California’s Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal impact: state budget reserves would be higher. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. Opponents: None submitted.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
61% yes
38% no
1% don’t know
21. [likely voters only] Proposition 3 is called “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.” It makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal impact: maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA. Opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
58% yes
41% no
1% don’t know
22. [likely voters only] Proposition 4 is called “Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.” It repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal impact: ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog. Opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; United Latinos Action.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
45% yes
52% no
3% don’t know
23. [likely voters only] Proposition 5 is called “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.” Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal impact: net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted. Opponents: None submitted.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
45% yes
52% no
3% don’t know
24. [likely voters only] Proposition 37 is called “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.” It authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not state. Fiscal impact: no direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma. Opponents: None submitted.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
65% yes
32% no
4% don’t know
25. [likely voters only] Proposition 38 is called “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute.” It authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal impact: increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Association; American Nurses Association of California. Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
57% yes
41% no
2% don’t know
26. [likely voters only] Proposition 39 is called “Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.” It invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal impact: costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Association; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association; CA Women’s Leadership Association. Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California.

41% yes
58% no
1% don’t know
27. [likely voters only] Proposition 40 is called “Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.” It imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal impact: temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West. Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association.

46% yes

28. [likely voters only] Proposition 41 is called “Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.” It nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal impact: the net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax). Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West.

29. [likely voters only] Proposition 42 is called “Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.” It prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayers’ past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, that conflict with this measure. Fiscal impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building and Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA. Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West.

51% yes

30. [likely voters only] Proposition 43 is called “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.” Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-imposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of voters needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce. Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.

Fiscal impact: increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted. Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Association.

Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative
Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office (https://oag.ca.gov/) who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents believe that The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative aims to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs by investing in immunotherapies that empower the patient's own immune system to target and combat disease. Supporters emphasize that because these therapies are already effectively treating certain cancers and chronic conditions, dedicated state funding will help move proven, cutting-edge science out of the research lab and into clinical treatments for patients more quickly.
The opposition argues that Proposition 38 is a deceptive measure designed to benefit its billionaire donor by funneling state resources toward a single institution using arbitrary criteria. Opponents contend that state funds for medical research should instead be allocated through a fair, competitive process where all eligible applicants have an equal opportunity to compete.

Welcome to the Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, Brew.
By: Lara Bonatesta
Here’s what’s in store for you as you start your day:

State Democratic and Republican parties took opposing positions on 70 ballot measures and agreed on six in 2026
Of the 164 statewide ballot measures that voters have or will decide this year, there were six that state Democratic and Republican parties agreed on and 70 that they disagreed on. Fifty-two measures received support or opposition from only one party. Thirty-six measures did not receive support or opposition from either party.
Republicans supported 50 that Democrats opposed, and Democrats supported 20 that Republicans opposed. Both parties agreed in their support of three measures and opposition to three others.
Overall, Republican parties supported 80 measures (48.8%), opposed 30 (18.3%), and were neutral or had no position on 54 (32.9%). Democratic parties supported 36 measures (22.0%), opposed 58 (35.4%), and were neutral or had no position on 70 (42.7%).
Voters will decide 145 measures on Nov. 3. The other 19 appeared on ballots earlier this year.
Of the 70 measures state parties disagreed on, legislators put 41 (58.6%) on the ballot, and 29 (41.4%) were citizen initiatives, including veto referendums. Some common issues the parties disagreed on were:
Voter ID (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_voter_ID,_2026) : Republicans supported and Democrats opposed measures in Arizona (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_144,_Voter_Identification_and_Citizenship_Voting_Requirements_Amendment_(2026)), California (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_39,_Voter_Identification,_Citizenship_Verification,_and_Registered_Voter_List_Administration_Initiative_(2026)), Colorado (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Amendment_84,_Require_Voter_Identification_Number_for_Mail-In_Ballots_Initiative_(2026)), North Carolina (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment_(2026)), and Ohio (https://ballotpedia.org/Ohio_Issue_3,_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment_(2026)) that would establish or expand voter identification requirements in state constitutions. The Nevada Republicans supported Question 7 (https://ballotpedia.org/Nevada_Question_7,_Require_Voter_Identification_Initiative_(2026)), with no position recorded for Democrats. The Oklahoma Democratic Party opposed State Question 846 (https://ballotpedia.org/Oklahoma_State_Question_846,_Voter_Identification_Requirement_Amendment_(August_2026)), with no position recorded for Republicans.
Abortion policy (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_abortion_policy,_2026) : Democrats supported and Republicans opposed measures in Idaho (https://ballotpedia.org/Idaho_Proposition_1,_Reproductive_Freedom_and_Privacy_Act_Initiative_(2026)) and Virginia (https://ballotpedia.org/Virginia_Question_1,_Right_to_Reproductive_Freedom_Amendment_(2026)), which would establish statutory and constitutional rights related to abortion, respectively. Republicans supported, and Democrats opposed, Missouri Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)), which would repeal the constitutional right to reproductive freedom voters approved in 2024 and prohibit abortion with specified exceptions, among other changes. The Nevada Democratic Party supported Question 6 (https://ballotpedia.org/Nevada_Question_6,_Right_to_Abortion_Initiative_(2026)), which would establish a constitutional right to abortion, with no position recorded for the Republican Party.
Sex-based school sports requirements (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_sex-based_sports_eligibility_and_medical_procedures_for_transgender_minors,_2026): Republicans supported and Democrats opposed all four measures that would establish sex-based requirements for school sports in Arizona (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_318,_Require_All_Schools_and_Athletic_Associations_to_Restrict_Sports_Participation_and_Access_to_Private_Spaces_Based_on_Sex_Measure_(2026)), Colorado (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_134,_Sex_Requirement_for_School_and_College_Sports_Initiative_(2026)), Nebraska (https://ballotpedia.org/Nebraska_Initiative_Measure_442,_Sex_Requirement_for_School_and_College_Sports_Initiative_(2026)), and Washington (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Initiative_638,_Sex_Verification_Requirements_for_Female_School_Sports_Initiative_(2026)).
Medical procedures for transgender minors (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_sex-based_sports_eligibility_and_medical_procedures_for_transgender_minors,_2026): Republicans supported and Democrats opposed Colorado Proposition 135 (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_135,_Prohibit_Surgeries_for_Treatment_in_Response_to_Minors%27_Perception_of_Sex_or_Gender_Measure_(2026)) and Missouri Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)), both of which would prohibit certain medical procedures for transgender minors.
Income and wealth taxes (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_income_and_wealth_taxes,_2026) : Democrats supported and Republicans opposed California Proposition 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)), which would extend higher-income tax rates for education funding; California Proposition 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)), which would impose a one-time wealth tax; and Colorado Amendment 87 (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Amendment_87,_Establish_Graduated_Income_Tax_and_Dedicate_New_Revenue_to_Education,_Healthcare,_and_Childcare_Initiative_(2026)), which would replace the flat income tax with graduated rates. Republicans supported and Democrats opposed measures to restrict, reduce, or repeal income or wealth taxes in California (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_(2026)), Colorado (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_136,_Establish_4.4%25_Cap_on_Individual_and_Corporate_Income_Tax_Rates_Initiative_(2026)), Iowa (https://ballotpedia.org/Iowa_Amendment_1,_Two-Thirds_Legislative_Vote_Requirement_for_Income_Tax_Increase_Bills_Amendment_(2026)), Missouri (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_5,_Income_Tax_Elimination_and_Sales_Tax_Changes_Amendment_(August_2026)), North Carolina (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Reduce_Income_Tax_Rate_Cap_from_7%25_to_3.5%25_Amendment_(2026)), and Washington (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Initiative_645,_Repeal_Tax_on_Household_Income_Over_$1_Million_and_Prohibit_State_and_Local_Taxes_on_Income_Initiative_(2026)).
Democratic and Republican parties in the same state supported:
California Proposition 38 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_38,_Immunology_and_Immunotherapy_Research_Funding_Initiative_(2026)), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Louisiana Amendment 7 (https://ballotpedia.org/Louisiana_Amendment_7,_Use_Public_Funds_for_Drinking_Water_Utility_Service_Lines_Amendment_(2026)) , which would amend the state constitution to authorize public funds for maintaining drinking water utility service lines affected by hazardous materials on property owned by utility customers.
Massachusetts Question 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_1,_Public_Records_Requirements_for_Legislature_and_Governor%E2%80%99s_Office_Initiative_(2026)), which would make records that the Legislature and governor’s office hold subject to the state’s public records law with certain exceptions.
Democratic and Republican parties in the same state opposed:
California Proposition 44 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_44,_Spending_Requirements_for_Federally_Qualified_Health_Centers_Initiative_(2026)), which would require nonprofit federally qualified health centers to spend at least 90% of their annual total revenue on expenses that advance the health center’s mission.
Colorado Proposition 137 (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_137,_Retain_Sporting_Goods_Sales_Tax_Revenue_for_Conservation_and_Wildfire_Prevention_Fund_Initiative_(2026)), which would allow the state to retain and spend sales tax revenue from sporting goods and equipment on water, land, forests, wildfire prevention, and outdoor recreation rather than refunding it under the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights (TABOR).
Massachusetts Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_3,_Top-Two_Primary_Elections_Initiative_(2026)), which would replace separate political party primaries for state elections with a single top-two primaries listing all candidates on the same ballot, regardless of political affiliation.
Legislative votes and party positions differed on five measures
State Democratic parties opposed two measures that Democratic state legislators largely supported in placing on the ballot. 96.3% of Democratic legislators supported California Proposition 43 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_43,_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Local_Special_Tax_Initiatives_and_Property_Tax_Initiative_Prohibition_Amendment_(2026)). It would require two-thirds voter approval for citizen-initiated local special taxes and prohibit local jurisdictions and ballot initiatives from enacting certain property taxes. 100% of Democratic legislators supported Utah Constitutional Amendment A (https://ballotpedia.org/Utah_Constitutional_Amendment_A,_Publication_Requirements_for_Constitutional_Amendments_Measure_(2026)). It would require proposed constitutional amendments to be published for 60 days before the election in a manner that the legislature specifies. It would replace the requirement for newspaper publication in each county.
State Republican parties opposed three measures that Republican state legislators largely supported in placing on the ballot. 100% of Republican legislators supported New Mexico’s Bond Question 2 (https://ballotpedia.org/New_Mexico_Bond_Question_2,_Library_Acquisition_Bond_Issue_(2026)) and Bond Question 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/New_Mexico_Bond_Question_3,_Higher_Education_Improvements_Bond_Issue_(2026)). Question 2 would authorize up to $20 million in bonds for academic, public school, tribal, and public library acquisitions. Question 3 would authorize up to $230 million in bonds for capital improvements and acquisitions at higher education institutions, special schools, and tribal schools. A statewide property tax would fund both bonds. 95.1% of Republican legislators supported Constitutional Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/New_Mexico_Board_of_Regents_Nominating_Committees_Amendment_(2026)). It would establish regents nominating committees, require student appointees to come from lists that student governing bodies provide, and prohibit non-student appointees from changing political parties during the 12 months preceding appointment.
No measures received state-party support when a majority of that party’s legislators voted against putting them on the ballot.
Click here (https://ballotpedia.org/State_Democratic_and_Republican_party_positions_on_ballot_measures,_2026) to read more about state Democratic and Republican party positions on ballot measures in 2026.
28 local ballot measures on Nov. 3 would limit data center development if approved, 13 would facilitate it
On Nov. 3, voters in 10 states will vote on 41 ballot measures affecting local data center policy.
A “yes” vote on 28 of these measures would limit data center development through policies such as bans or moratoriums. A “yes” vote on the remaining 13 measures would facilitate data center development through policies like zoning.
Voters have already decided six measures this year and, in each case, a majority of voters favored greater limits on data center development, either by approving new restrictions or requirements or by rejecting a measure that would have facilitated or supported development. Including these measures, and three that voters will decide after Nov. 3, Ballotpedia is covering 50 local ballot measures (https://ballotpedia.org/Data_center-related_ballot_measures,_2026) in 13 states related to data centers this year.
Ohio voters will decide on 21 measures, more than any other state. Illinois follows with seven measures. Maine voters will decide four, and Kansas voters will decide three. Voters in California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, and Wisconsin will decide one each.
State policies on data centers
State and local governments can affect data center construction through policy actions like permitting, zoning, and tax incentives. As of April 2026, 38 states (https://www.ncsl.org/state-legislatures-news/details/does-your-state-offer-data-center-tax-incentives) had created tax incentives to encourage data center construction.
State and local governments can also use some of these policy actions to prevent or limit data center construction, for example through moratoriums (temporary halts) on issuing permits for new projects. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (https://ballotpedia.org/Kathy_Hochul) (D) issued (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/14/nyregion/new-york-data-center-moratorium-hochul.html) an executive order (https://www.governor.ny.gov/sites/default/files/2026-07/EO_62.pdf) for the first state-level moratorium on data center construction. This one-year moratorium barred state regulators from issuing permits for new data centers expected to use 50 megawatts or more of electricity. Other states have also issued moratoriums on administrative measures like tax breaks (https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/gov-jb-pritzker-to-suspend-tax-breaks-for-data-centers-urging-more-discussion/) and environmental permits (https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/21/texas-data-center-moratorium-water-energy/) for data center construction.
What the Nov. 3 ballot measures would do
Twenty-eight measures, if approved, would limit data center development:
Seventeen would ban data centers. Twelve of these would ban data centers above a certain size threshold. For example, one measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Ottawa,_Kansas,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Kansas would ban data centers using more than 25 megawatts of electricity. Five would ban all data centers.
Three would issue six-month moratoriums on data center development. One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Wells,_Maine,_Article_5,_Data_Center_Moratorium_Measure_(November_2026)) for a moratorium in Wells, Maine, would also (https://wellstown.org/DocumentCenter/View/8514/November-3-2026-Special-Town-Meeting-Warrant?bidId=&p=9) retroactively "nullify any final permit, license, or other approval of a new or expanded Data Center issued by a municipal reviewing authority within 45 days of the effective date."
Two measures in Ohio would establish zoning regulations for unincorporated areas of the local jurisdictions. If the measures are successful and the areas are covered by zoning regulations, they would have to be zoned for a use consistent with data center construction (such as industrial) for a project to be built there.
One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Grove_City,_Ohio,_Issue_28,_Voter_Approval_Requirements_for_Certain_Developments_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Ohio would require voter approval for data center projects above land, water, and power use thresholds, while another (https://ballotpedia.org/Janesville,_Wisconsin,_Require_Voter_Approval_for_Development_of_GM/JATCO_Site_Exceeding_$450_Million_Initiative_(November_2026)) measure in Wisconsin would require voter approval for a specific data center project if it costs more than $450 million.
A measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Harwood,_North_Dakota,_Industrial_Development_Review_Requirements_Initiative_(November_2026)) in North Dakota would require independent professional review and a public hearing for projects exceeding various land area, power, and water use thresholds, as well as projects requiring a major air quality permit.
A measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Perry,_Ohio,_Issue_16,_Hyperscale_Data_Center_Tax_Incentive_Financial_Guarantee_Requirement_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Ohio would require data center developers receiving tax incentives to provide financial guarantees to the community.
Two non-binding measures in Illinois would express voter disapproval of data center projects.
Thirteen measures, if approved, would facilitate data center development:
One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Boulder_City,_Nevada,_Question_1,_Allow_Data_Centers_in_Eldorado_Valley_Transfer_Area_Measure_(November_2026)) in Nevada would add data centers as an approved use for a particular area of land.
One (https://ballotpedia.org/Ashville,_Ohio,_Data_Center_EdgeConneX_Development_Term_Summary_Referendum_(November_2026)) measure in Ohio would uphold a town agreement with a specific data center company.
Four measures in Wilmington, Ohio would rezone specific areas of land from residential to industrial uses, allowing data center construction at these sites. According to WCPO News (https://www.wcpo.com/news/local-news/wilmington-residents-take-aim-at-industrial-zoning-for-data-centers-with-ballot-referendum), a specific data center company may build on this land if it is rezoned.
Seven non-binding measures in Illinois, New Jersey, and Ohio would express voter approval of data center projects.
Voters in four states have already voted on six data center-related measures.
On March 10, voters in Canterbury, New Hampshire, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Canterbury,_New_Hampshire,_Article_4,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Measure_(March_2026)) a ban on data centers 83.6% to 16.4%.
On April 7, voters in Port Washington, Wisconsin, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Port_Washington,_Wisconsin,_Require_Voter_Approval_for_Tax_Incremental_Districts_Exceeding_$10_Million_Initiative_(April_2026)) an initiative 66.4% to 33.6% requiring voter approval for the city to create a Tax Incremental District if projects in the district cost $10 million or more.
On June 2, voters in Monterey Park, California, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Monterey_Park,_California,_Measure_NDC,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Measure_(June_2026)) a ban 88.3% to 11.7%.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

# Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
## Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
### Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026.
To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures.
On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund.
The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent.
The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi- Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures- Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)- giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.
PROPOSAL
New Bond for Specified Medical Research. Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.
Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
Requires Purchases From California Suppliers. Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
Requires California Patient Discount. Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years . The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries. The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 38
California should continue supporting biomedical research. Everyone hopes for new treatments for heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and other serious illnesses. I do too. But Proposition 38 is the wrong way to achieve that goal.
The claim that Proposition 38 will pay for itself is speculative. Audits, public disclosure, and limits on administrative costs promote accountability, but they cannot guarantee that research investments will generate enough economic returns to offset billions of dollars in bond repayments.
California faces a continuing structural budget deficit.
Proposition 38 would require approximately $8.4 billion in bond repayments. According to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, taxpayers would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years. That long-term obligation would further reduce the state’s fiscal flexibility to respond to changing priorities.
Meanwhile, recent actions by the Trump administration have placed funding for essential California public health programs at risk, including disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, HIV prevention, vaccination infrastructure, laboratory capacity, and community prevention. These challenges extend well beyond biomedical research.
If California chooses to replace declining federal support, elected officials should be able to consider all health priorities together. Proposition 38 instead earmarks billions of borrowed dollars for one scientific field, regardless of future needs or discoveries. Research priorities should be guided through the normal budget process-not by ballot measures that lock taxpayers into decades of debt. Vote No on Proposition 38.

ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 38
California recognizes that continued investment in science is essential. But this proposition is not the best way to achieve that goal.
The measure would authorize approximately $8.4 billion in state borrowing to support immunology and immunotherapy research through a new University of California institute. Although the objective is appealing, the financing and policy framework are flawed.
First, the proposition continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics. California has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine. This measure would add another highly focused program. Research priorities should be established through scientific review and public health planning-not by election campaigns. Cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and heart disease deserve attention, but so do mental illness, kidney disease, eye diseases, and many other conditions. Ballot-box science inevitably favors the most visible topics rather than the greatest scientific opportunities or public health needs.
Second, borrowing is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the bonds authorized by this measure would obligate taxpayers to $500 million in annual debt payments for about 25 years. Bonds are commonly used for highways, schools, and other long-lived infrastructure with predictable benefits. Scientific research is different. Discoveries often require decades before they improve patient care, and many promising lines of investigation never produce marketable treatments.
Third, the proposition assumes that successful discoveries will generate revenues to offset state costs. In reality, universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own. Publicly funded research lays the scientific foundation, but private companies typically invest the far greater resources required for product development, clinical testing, manufacturing, and regulatory approval. The public benefits are real, but they generally do not flow back to the state treasury.
Finally, the proposition requires certain therapies developed with state support to be sold in California at discounted prices. While this may sound attractive, it could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states where the prices are not controlled.
California should continue to support biomedical research. But research funding should be strategic, flexible, and fiscally responsible. Decisions about scientific priorities should be based on expert evaluation of emerging scientific opportunities and public health needs, not on a series of expensive ballot measures financed through long-term debt.
California has better options. For example, Senator Scott Wiener has proposed creating a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. Rather than directing resources to specific areas of science, such an institution could establish priorities through expert scientific review and adapt its investments as new opportunities emerge. Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California, the United Auto Workers, and the Union of American Physicians and Dentists. Similar legislation is likely to be considered in the future.
A “No” vote does not reject science. It rejects an inefficient financing mechanism and a fragmented approach to setting research priorities. California can and should support medical research through more coordinated, sustainable policies.
Robert M Kaplan , Ph.D.

Prop 38 Frequently Asked Questions
What does a YES vote on Prop 38 mean?
A YES vote on Prop 38 means California will support $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology research (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at California universities and nonprofit research institutions to find cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease and other devastating diseases in our lifetime. Prop 38 is designed to pay for itself, with 10% of proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies developed from Prop 38 funding returned to the state (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm). Additionally, California patients will get a 20% discount on the cures it helps create (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
Copy link for this answer Copied!
Where will the research funded by Prop 38 happen?
Medical research funded by Prop 38 will be conducted here in California at leading universities and medical research institutions (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) that are well-qualified to conduct breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research.
That may include University of California campuses, such as UCLA, UC Berkeley, UC San Diego, UC San Francisco, UC Irvine, UC Davis, and UC Riverside; private non-profit universities, such as Stanford, USC and Caltech; and non-profit research institutions such as City of Hope, Cedars-Sinai, and Sanford Burnham Prebys, among others.
No funds from Prop 38 can be awarded to pharmaceutical companies or other for-profit corporations. (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
Copy link for this answer Copied!
Will Prop 38 make medical treatments more affordable for Californians?
Yes. Any cure or immunotherapy developed through research funded by Prop 38 must be made available to California patients at a 20% discount below the national average (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf). That affordability protection is written directly into the measure — it’s not optional.
Copy link for this answer Copied!
How will Prop 38 be paid for?
Prop 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers (https://yeson38.com/myths-vs-facts/#can-california-afford). Ten percent (10%) of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies must be returned to the State of California (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) to offset the total cost of the bond measure, including interest. Furthermore, preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term healthcare expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Copy link for this answer Copied!
How does Prop 38 ensure oversight and accountability?
Prop 38 includes strong accountability and transparency requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), including limiting state administrative costs to run the program to no more than 2% (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm), requiring all grant funds to nonprofit universities and research centers be spent directly on medical research, rigorous conflict of interest rules, public disclosure of all spending and independent financial audits.
