When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). The DSF-based sampling frame used for address selection is enhanced with a series of refinements—such as the appendage of various ancillary d

ata to each address from commercial and government data sources—to facilitate complex stratification plans. Taking advantage of such refinements, quarterly samples are selected using a stratified sampling methodology that aims to retain the representativeness of the panel. KnowledgePanel recruits new panel members throughout the year to offset panel attrition.
To qualify for the survey, a panel member must be age 18 or older and reside in California. A general population sample of Californians was selected using Ipsos’s PPS (probability proportional to size) sampling procedure to select study-specific samples. Briefly, to select such samples, the panel is first weighted to population benchmarks and those panel weights are used as the measure of size for a PPS sample selection that yields a fully representative sample. A total of 1,800 respondents completed the survey out of 3,046 panelists who were sampled, for a response rate of 59 percent. To ensure the highest data quality, we flagged respondents who sped through the survey, which we defined as completing the survey in one-fourth of the overall median time (less than 3.5 minutes). We also flagged respondents if their self-reported age or gender did not match the data stored in their profile. A total of 72 cases were removed after this review process, resulting in 1,728 total qualified and valid cases.
Accent on Languages, Inc., translated new survey questions into Spanish, with assistance from Renatta DeFever.
We use the US Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey’s (ACS) Public Use Microdata Series for California (with regional coding information from the University of Minnesota’s Integrated Public Use Microdata Series for California) to compare certain demographic characteristics of the survey sample—region, age, gender, race/ethnicity, education, and income—with the characteristics of California’s adult population. The survey sample was closely comparable to the ACS figures. We also used voter registration data from the California Secretary of State to compare the party registration of registered voters in our sample to party registration statewide. The sample of Californians is first weighted using an initial sampling or base weight that corrects for any differences in the probability of selecting various segments of the KnowledgePanel sample. This base weight is further adjusted using an iterative proportional fitting (raking) procedure that aligns sample demographics to population benchmarks from the 2024 ACS data as well as party registration benchmarks from the California Secretary of State’s voter registration file.
The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the total unweighted sample of 1,728 adults. This means that 95 times out of 100, the results will be within 3 percentage points of what they would be if all adults in California were interviewed. The sampling error for unweighted subgroups is larger: for the 1,449 registered voters, the sampling error is ±3.3 percent; for the 1,086 likely voters, it is ±3.8 percent. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording, question order, and survey timing.
We present results for five geographic regions, accounting for approximately 90 percent of the state population. “Central Valley” includes Butte, Colusa, El Dorado, Fresno, Glenn, Kern, Kings, Madera, Merced, Placer, Sacramento, San Joaquin, Shasta, Stanislaus, Sutter, Tehama, Tulare, Yolo, and Yuba Counties. “San Francisco Bay Area” includes Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano, and Sonoma Counties. “Los Angeles” refers to Los Angeles County, “Inland Empire” refers to Riverside and San Bernardino Counties, and “Orange/San Diego” refers to Orange and San Diego Counties. Residents of other geographic areas are included in the results reported for all adults, registered voters, and likely voters, but sample sizes for these less-populous areas are not large enough to report separately.
We present results for non-Hispanic whites, who account for 35 percent of the state’s adult population, and also for Latinos, who account for 38 percent of the state’s adult population and constitute one of the fastest-growing voter groups. We also present results for non-Hispanic Asian Americans, who make up about 17 percent of the state’s adult population, and non-Hispanic African Americans, who comprise about 5 percent. Results for other racial/ethnic groups—such as Native Americans—are included in the results reported for all adults, registered voters, and likely voters, but sample sizes are not large enough for separate analysis. Results for African American and Asian American likely voters are combined with those of other racial/ethnic groups because sample sizes for African American and Asian American likely voters are too small for separate analysis. We compare the opinions of those who report they are registered Democrats, registered Republicans, and decline-to-state or independent voters; the results for those who say they are registered to vote in other parties are not large enough for separate analysis. We also analyze the responses of likely voters—so designated per their responses to survey questions about voter registration, previous election participation, intentions to vote this year, attention to election news, and current interest in politics.

01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.

One more question
Why less sunlight for billions in public money?
Despite promises of accountability, the selected institute would not be treated as a public agency under key California transparency and ethics laws, including the Public Records Act, open-meeting requirements and the Political Reform Act.
Public money should come with full public accountability.
Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. CalMatters reported that its eligibility criteria very likely point to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder and board chair is the largest financial backer of Proposition 38.
What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.
What should California do instead? Use independent scientific review and open competition to fund the strongest proposals across institutions and fields. Research priorities should be able to change as evidence, technology and public-health needs evolve.
Sources: California Legislative Analyst (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026) and CalMatters reporting (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/).

[randomize response options]

Next, we have a few questions to ask you about the state propositions on the November ballot.
19. [likely voters only] Proposition 1 is called “Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.” It authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and down payment assistance. Fiscal impact: increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child and Family Services. Opponents: None submitted.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
60% yes
38% no
2% don’t know
20. [likely voters only] Proposition 2 is called “Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.” It increases California’s Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal impact: state budget reserves would be higher. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. Opponents: None submitted.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
61% yes
38% no
1% don’t know
21. [likely voters only] Proposition 3 is called “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.” It makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education. Fiscal impact: maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031. Supporters: California Teachers Association; CA School Nurses Organization; California State PTA; Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA. Opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
58% yes
41% no
1% don’t know
22. [likely voters only] Proposition 4 is called “Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.” It repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal impact: ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog. Opponents: California Taxpayers Association; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; United Latinos Action.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
45% yes
52% no
3% don’t know
23. [likely voters only] Proposition 5 is called “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.” Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal impact: net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted. Opponents: None submitted.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
45% yes
52% no
3% don’t know
24. [likely voters only] Proposition 37 is called “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.” It authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not state. Fiscal impact: no direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma. Opponents: None submitted.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
65% yes
32% no
4% don’t know
25. [likely voters only] Proposition 38 is called “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute.” It authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal impact: increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Association; American Nurses Association of California. Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
57% yes
41% no
2% don’t know
26. [likely voters only] Proposition 39 is called “Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.” It invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal impact: costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Association; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association; CA Women’s Leadership Association. Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
41% yes
58% no
1% don’t know
27. [likely voters only] Proposition 40 is called “Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.” It imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal impact: temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West. Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
46% yes
52% no
2% don’t know
28. [likely voters only] Proposition 41 is called “Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.” It nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal impact: the net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax). Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
48% yes
49% no
3% don’t know
29. [likely voters only] Proposition 42 is called “Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.” It prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayers’ past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, that conflict with this measure. Fiscal impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building and Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA. Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
51% yes
47% no
2% don’t know
30. [likely voters only] Proposition 43 is called “Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.” Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-imposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of voters needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. Supporters: California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce. Opponents: California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
42% yes
55% no
3% don’t know
31. [likely voters only] Proposition 44 is called “Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.” It imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal impact: increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted. Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Association.
If the election were held today, would you vote yes or no?
25% yes
71% no
4% don’t know
32. [likely voters only] Proposition 45 is called “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.” It amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal impact: initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing. Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation.

Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative
Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office (https://oag.ca.gov/) who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents believe that The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative aims to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs by investing in immunotherapies that empower the patient's own immune system to target and combat disease. Supporters emphasize that because these therapies are already effectively treating certain cancers and chronic conditions, dedicated state funding will help move proven, cutting-edge science out of the research lab and into clinical treatments for patients more quickly.
The opposition argues that Proposition 38 is a deceptive measure designed to benefit its billionaire donor by funneling state resources toward a single institution using arbitrary criteria. Opponents contend that state funds for medical research should instead be allocated through a fair, competitive process where all eligible applicants have an equal opportunity to compete.

State Democratic and Republican parties took opposing positions on 70 ballot measures and agreed on six in 2026
Of the 164 statewide ballot measures that voters have or will decide this year, there were six that state Democratic and Republican parties agreed on and 70 that they disagreed on. Fifty-two measures received support or opposition from only one party. Thirty-six measures did not receive support or opposition from either party.
Republicans supported 50 that Democrats opposed, and Democrats supported 20 that Republicans opposed. Both parties agreed in their support of three measures and opposition to three others.
Overall, Republican parties supported 80 measures (48.8%), opposed 30 (18.3%), and were neutral or had no position on 54 (32.9%). Democratic parties supported 36 measures (22.0%), opposed 58 (35.4%), and were neutral or had no position on 70 (42.7%).
Voters will decide 145 measures on Nov. 3. The other 19 appeared on ballots earlier this year.
Of the 70 measures state parties disagreed on, legislators put 41 (58.6%) on the ballot, and 29 (41.4%) were citizen initiatives, including veto referendums. Some common issues the parties disagreed on were:
Voter ID (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_voter_ID,_2026) : Republicans supported and Democrats opposed measures in Arizona (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_144,_Voter_Identification_and_Citizenship_Voting_Requirements_Amendment_(2026)), California (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_39,_Voter_Identification,_Citizenship_Verification,_and_Registered_Voter_List_Administration_Initiative_(2026)), Colorado (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Amendment_84,_Require_Voter_Identification_Number_for_Mail-In_Ballots_Initiative_(2026)), North Carolina (https://ballotpedia.org/North_Carolina_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment_(2026)), and Ohio (https://ballotpedia.org/Ohio_Issue_3,_Require_Voter_Identification_Amendment_(2026)) that would establish or expand voter identification requirements in state constitutions. The Nevada Republicans supported Question 7 (https://ballotpedia.org/Nevada_Question_7,_Require_Voter_Identification_Initiative_(2026)), with no position recorded for Democrats. The Oklahoma Democratic Party opposed State Question 846 (https://ballotpedia.org/Oklahoma_State_Question_846,_Voter_Identification_Requirement_Amendment_(August_2026)), with no position recorded for Republicans.
Abortion policy (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_abortion_policy,_2026) : Democrats supported and Republicans opposed measures in Idaho (https://ballotpedia.org/Idaho_Proposition_1,_Reproductive_Freedom_and_Privacy_Act_Initiative_(2026)) and Virginia (https://ballotpedia.org/Virginia_Question_1,_Right_to_Reproductive_Freedom_Amendment_(2026)), which would establish statutory and constitutional rights related to abortion, respectively. Republicans supported, and Democrats opposed, Missouri Amendment 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/Missouri_Amendment_3,_Prohibit_Abortion_and_Gender_Transition_Procedures_for_Minors_Amendment_(2026)), which would repeal the constitutional right to reproductive freedom voters approved in 2024 and prohibit abortion with specified exceptions, among other changes. The Nevada Democratic Party supported Question 6 (https://ballotpedia.org/Nevada_Question_6,_Right_to_Abortion_Initiative_(2026)), which would establish a constitutional right to abortion, with no position recorded for the Republican Party.
Sex-based school sports requirements (https://ballotpedia.org/Ballot_measures_related_to_sex-based_sports_eligibility_and_medical_procedures_for_transgender_minors,_2026): Republicans supported and Democrats opposed all four measures that would establish sex-based requirements for school sports in Arizona (https://ballotpedia.org/Arizona_Proposition_318,_Require_All_Schools_and_Athletic_Associations_to_Restrict_Sports_Participation_and_Access_to_Private_Spaces_Based_on_Sex_Measure_(2026)), Colorado (https://ballotpedia.org/Colorado_Proposition_134,_Sex_Requirement_for_School_and_College_Sports_Initiative_(2026)), Nebraska (https://ballotpedia.org/Nebraska_Initiative_Measure_442,_Sex_Requirement_for_School_and_College_Sports_Initiative_(2026)), and Washington (https://ballotpedia.org/Washington_Initiative_638,_Sex_Verification_Requirements_for_Female_School_Sports_Initiative_(2026)).

28 local ballot measures on Nov. 3 would limit data center development if approved, 13 would facilitate it
On Nov. 3, voters in 10 states will vote on 41 ballot measures affecting local data center policy.
A “yes” vote on 28 of these measures would limit data center development through policies such as bans or moratoriums. A “yes” vote on the remaining 13 measures would facilitate data center development through policies like zoning.
Voters have already decided six measures this year and, in each case, a majority of voters favored greater limits on data center development, either by approving new restrictions or requirements or by rejecting a measure that would have facilitated or supported development. Including these measures, and three that voters will decide after Nov. 3, Ballotpedia is covering 50 local ballot measures (https://ballotpedia.org/Data_center-related_ballot_measures,_2026) in 13 states related to data centers this year.
Ohio voters will decide on 21 measures, more than any other state. Illinois follows with seven measures. Maine voters will decide four, and Kansas voters will decide three. Voters in California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, and Wisconsin will decide one each.
State policies on data centers
State and local governments can affect data center construction through policy actions like permitting, zoning, and tax incentives. As of April 2026, 38 states (https://www.ncsl.org/state-legislatures-news/details/does-your-state-offer-data-center-tax-incentives) had created tax incentives to encourage data center construction.
State and local governments can also use some of these policy actions to prevent or limit data center construction, for example through moratoriums (temporary halts) on issuing permits for new projects. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (https://ballotpedia.org/Kathy_Hochul) (D) issued (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/14/nyregion/new-york-data-center-moratorium-hochul.html) an executive order (https://www.governor.ny.gov/sites/default/files/2026-07/EO_62.pdf) for the first state-level moratorium on data center construction. This one-year moratorium barred state regulators from issuing permits for new data centers expected to use 50 megawatts or more of electricity. Other states have also issued moratoriums on administrative measures like tax breaks (https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/gov-jb-pritzker-to-suspend-tax-breaks-for-data-centers-urging-more-discussion/) and environmental permits (https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/21/texas-data-center-moratorium-water-energy/) for data center construction.
What the Nov. 3 ballot measures would do
Twenty-eight measures, if approved, would limit data center development:
Seventeen would ban data centers. Twelve of these would ban data centers above a certain size threshold. For example, one measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Ottawa,_Kansas,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Kansas would ban data centers using more than 25 megawatts of electricity. Five would ban all data centers.
Three would issue six-month moratoriums on data center development. One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Wells,_Maine,_Article_5,_Data_Center_Moratorium_Measure_(November_2026)) for a moratorium in Wells, Maine, would also (https://wellstown.org/DocumentCenter/View/8514/November-3-2026-Special-Town-Meeting-Warrant?bidId=&p=9) retroactively "nullify any final permit, license, or other approval of a new or expanded Data Center issued by a municipal reviewing authority within 45 days of the effective date."
Two measures in Ohio would establish zoning regulations for unincorporated areas of the local jurisdictions. If the measures are successful and the areas are covered by zoning regulations, they would have to be zoned for a use consistent with data center construction (such as industrial) for a project to be built there.
One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Grove_City,_Ohio,_Issue_28,_Voter_Approval_Requirements_for_Certain_Developments_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Ohio would require voter approval for data center projects above land, water, and power use thresholds, while another (https://ballotpedia.org/Janesville,_Wisconsin,_Require_Voter_Approval_for_Development_of_GM/JATCO_Site_Exceeding_$450_Million_Initiative_(November_2026)) measure in Wisconsin would require voter approval for a specific data center project if it costs more than $450 million.
A measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Harwood,_North_Dakota,_Industrial_Development_Review_Requirements_Initiative_(November_2026)) in North Dakota would require independent professional review and a public hearing for projects exceeding various land area, power, and water use thresholds, as well as projects requiring a major air quality permit.
A measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Perry,_Ohio,_Issue_16,_Hyperscale_Data_Center_Tax_Incentive_Financial_Guarantee_Requirement_Initiative_(November_2026)) in Ohio would require data center developers receiving tax incentives to provide financial guarantees to the community.
Two non-binding measures in Illinois would express voter disapproval of data center projects.
Thirteen measures, if approved, would facilitate data center development:
One measure (https://ballotpedia.org/Boulder_City,_Nevada,_Question_1,_Allow_Data_Centers_in_Eldorado_Valley_Transfer_Area_Measure_(November_2026)) in Nevada would add data centers as an approved use for a particular area of land.
One (https://ballotpedia.org/Ashville,_Ohio,_Data_Center_EdgeConneX_Development_Term_Summary_Referendum_(November_2026)) measure in Ohio would uphold a town agreement with a specific data center company.
Four measures in Wilmington, Ohio would rezone specific areas of land from residential to industrial uses, allowing data center construction at these sites. According to WCPO News (https://www.wcpo.com/news/local-news/wilmington-residents-take-aim-at-industrial-zoning-for-data-centers-with-ballot-referendum), a specific data center company may build on this land if it is rezoned.
Seven non-binding measures in Illinois, New Jersey, and Ohio would express voter approval of data center projects.
Voters in four states have already voted on six data center-related measures.
On March 10, voters in Canterbury, New Hampshire, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Canterbury,_New_Hampshire,_Article_4,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Measure_(March_2026)) a ban on data centers 83.6% to 16.4%.
On April 7, voters in Port Washington, Wisconsin, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Port_Washington,_Wisconsin,_Require_Voter_Approval_for_Tax_Incremental_Districts_Exceeding_$10_Million_Initiative_(April_2026)) an initiative 66.4% to 33.6% requiring voter approval for the city to create a Tax Incremental District if projects in the district cost $10 million or more.
On June 2, voters in Monterey Park, California, approved (https://ballotpedia.org/Monterey_Park,_California,_Measure_NDC,_Prohibit_Data_Centers_Measure_(June_2026)) a ban 88.3% to 11.7%.
